His coalition later obtained an absolute majority in both federal chambers.", "question_ids": ["5B.1", "6B.1", "8B.1", "8B.2", "8B.3"], "polarity": "context", "period_fit": "The program and electoral mandate predate 2023 and are relevant as frozen goals and authority baseline.", "ruler_attribution": "The program was López Obrador’s and the majorities belonged to his coalition.", "limitations": ["The source does not establish that the civilian-command security goal was achieved."], "start_unit": 19, "end_unit": 20, "locator": "extracted HTML block 19 through extracted HTML block 20", "exact_excerpt": "A lo largo de 2017 López Obrador, cabeza en todas las encuestas de intención de voto, terminó de perfilar su estrategia de cara a la gran prueba electoral de 2018. En junio, durante el III Congreso Nacional del partido, y luego del reclutamiento para MORENA de los ex presidentes perredistas Leonel Godoy y Leonel Cota (a los que en enero de 2018 iba a seguir Marcelo Ebrard, fichaje estrella de la formación izquierdista), el dirigente desestimó, por una cuestión de \"valores y principios\", la oferta hecha por la presidenta del PRD, Alejandra Barrales Magdaleno, y Miguel Ángel Mancera de acudir juntos a las elecciones federales en un frente amplio de izquierda. Entonces,\nAMLO\ndescartó explícitamente cualquier alianza preelectoral con el PRD, el PRI, el PAN, el PVEM, el PANAL, el PES y el MC, por tratarse de partidos \"al servicio del régimen\", y solo aprobó una coalición con el PT.\nEn el IV Congreso Nacional Extraordinario de MORENA, el 20 de noviembre de 2017, López Obrador hizo presentación del\nProyecto Alternativo de Nación 2018-2024\n, documento base para un plan de Gobierno abierto al escrutinio y debate de simpatizantes y ciudadanos, los cuales eran invitados al aporte de diagnósticos, ideas y propuestas. Terminado de ajustar como Proyecto 18 y con Alfonso Romo Garza de coordinador general, el documento se estructuraba en cuatro comisiones temáticas, a saber, Economía y Desarrollo, Desarrollo Social, Política y Gobierno, y Educación, Valores, Cultura y Ciencia, y presentaba siete lineamientos generales, cuales eran: Legalidad y erradicación de la corrupción; Combate a la pobreza; Recuperación de la paz; Viabilidad financiera y austeridad; Equidad de género; Desarrollo sostenible y buen vivir; y Reconstrucción nacional.\nA continuación, MORENA, el PT de Alberto Anaya Gutiérrez y el PES de Hugo Éric Flores Cervantes formalizaron la coalición Juntos Haremos Historia, con López Obrador de precandidato presidencial conjunto. A pesar de lo asegurado en junio, el morenista accedió a compartir cancha electoral con un partido, Encuentro Social, habitualmente descrito como de derecha religiosa y, por cierto, la antítesis del socialista y estrictamente laico PT.\nEste entendimiento fue interpretado como una muestra del creciente pragmatismo de López Obrador y también como el reconocimiento implícito de, a título personal, una cierta proximidad ideológica al evangélico Flores en temas de fe y moralidad. El líder nacional de MORENA se definía a sí mismo como cristiano \"en la extensión amplia de lo que significa el cristianismo\" y \"seguidor de la vida y la obra de Jesucristo\". Su postura más bien conservadora en materia de costumbres sociales era sugerida por su ambigüedad o evasivas cuando se le preguntaba por su opinión sobre cuestiones tales como la despenalización del aborto, el matrimonio igualitario y la adopción homoparental.\nEl 12 de diciembre de 2017 López Obrador se registró como precandidato presidencial ante la Comisión Nacional de Elecciones de MORENA. Desde este momento, la presidencia del CEN del partido quedaba en manos de la secretaria general, Yeidckol Polevnsky. Ahora mismo, el izquierdista era el primero en las encuestas con un 30% de apoyos. El último paso oficial fue la inscripción ante el INE como candidato por la coalición tripartita Juntos Haremos Historia, el 16 de marzo de 2018. En su discurso de registro,\nAMLO\nvislumbró el advenimiento de la \"Cuarta Transformación en la historia de México\", transformación que ellos iban a lograr \"sin violencia, de manera pacífica, con información y orientación, con la difusión de principios éticos, liberando a nuestros conciudadanos del miedo y la desinformación, y llamando a todas y todos a buscar la reconciliación\".\nEl candidato se refirió también a la necesidad de un \"gobierno honesto que represente a todos\", de lograr \"el renacimiento económico, social político y, sobre todo, moral de nuestro querido México\", y de asentar \"un auténtico Estado democrático de derecho\". Ellos no compartían la máxima de \"ni perdón ni olvido\": un Gobierno de MORENA acabaría ciertamente con \"la corrupción, la impunidad y los lujos en el Gobierno\", pero los \"integrantes del poder económico y político\" del país debían de saber que \"no les guardamos rencor y les aseguramos que tras su posible derrota no habrá represalias, ni persecución, ni destierro para nadie\". \"Declaramos enfáticamente que lo que se necesita es justicia, no venganza, no odiamos a nadie\", recalcó el candidato.\nEn estos momentos, mediados de marzo de 2018, López Obrador superaba holgadamente a sus principales competidores: por la coalición oficialista Todos por México (PRI, PVEM y PANAL), el capitalino José Antonio Meade Kuribreña, uno de los pesos pesados del equipo de Peña Nieto, del que había sido sucesivamente secretario de Relaciones Exteriores, secretario de Desarrollo Social y Secretario de Hacienda y Crédito Público; y, por la coalición Por México al Frente (PAN, PRD y MC), el mexiquense Ricardo Anaya Cortés, ex diputado federal y dos veces presidente de los panistas entre 2014 y 2017. En los muestreos de intención de voto la delantera del morenista oscilaba entre los 20 y los 30 puntos. Para muchos comentaristas, esta abultada ventaja de López Obrador era irreversible, más al no existir en México el sistema de la doble vuelta.\n10. Victoria histórica en las presidenciales de 2008\nHasta las elecciones federales del 1 de julio, López Obrador, Morena y Juntos Haremos Historia fueron desgranando las claves de su programa de Gobierno.\nEl programa electoral incidía en una serie de temas.\nEn primer lugar, se abogaba por la \"austeridad republicana\", un ajuste fiscal ligado al ahorro de gastos corrientes del Estado y la reorientación de los recursos públicos a la inversión, sin subir ningún impuesto (y sí bajando algunos, pero sólo en los estados fronterizos con Estados Unidos) y sin emitir deuda. Habría un aumento gradual del salario mínimo, hasta los 171 pesos al final del sexenio, y lo mismo para las pensiones de adultos mayores, que cobrarían mensualidades de 1.500 pesos. Se incrementaría la oferta de gasolina autóctona para reducir las importaciones y rebajar los precios, lo que requería poner en servicio más refinerías. La reforma energética de Peña Nieto sería sometida a una revisión a fondo, anulando y revirtiendo cuanto fuera necesario. Igualmente, se buscaría las autosuficiencias energética y alimentaria, en el caso del agro ofreciendo a los productores locales precios de garantía.\nEn el angustioso capítulo de la inseguridad, el Estado prestaría atención a las \"causas sociales\" de la violencia, lo que pasaba por combatir la pobreza y elevar el desarrollo humano de los colectivos vulnerables. Se asumía el principio de la retirada de las Fuerzas Armadas de las misiones de seguridad interna pero sin precipitaciones, mientras se organizase y desplegase un nuevo cuerpo armado, la Guardia Nacional, con la meta de \"pacificar\" México en tres años. Por otro lado, MORENA hablaba de \"erradicar\" la corrupción política \"dando ejemplo\" institucional desde Los Pinos.\nEl candidato entonó asimismo la defensa firme de los migrantes mexicanos, más en tiempos de muro fronterizo de Trump, aranceles unilaterales a las exportaciones mexicanas de metales al vecino norteño y renegociación forzada del TLCAN, para lo que buscaría establecer con Estados Unidos unas relaciones de cooperación y buena vecindad basadas \"en el respeto mutuo\". En marzo de 2018 López Obrador y Polevnsky repitieron que MORENA quería que México dispusiera del mejor equipo de negociadores para conseguir que el tratado que sucediera al TLCAN de 1992 fuera lo más favorable posible a los intereses nacionales. Por otro lado y de nuevo, el candidato salió a desacreditar los intentos de establecer una relación simpática entre su plataforma y el régimen de Caracas: él no tenía \"nada que ver con el Gobierno de Venezuela\", y su \"mexicanismo\" equivalía a decir \"ni chavismo, ni trumpismo\", recalcó.\nLa plataforma lopezobradorista para el período de gobierno 2018-2024 sugería una socialdemocracia pragmática que ni comulgaba con la teoría de la lucha de clases del socialismo ni aspiraba a volver a los esquemas proteccionistas o estatistas del viejo PRI. Al contrario, asumía los principios ortodoxos del libre mercado, el libre comercio, la estabilidad macroeconómica, la disciplina presupuestaria, la flotación del peso y la autonomía del Banco de México, pero conjugadas, eso sí, con el rechazo al \"neoliberalismo\", las \"tendencias privatizadoras\" y la \"extranjerización\" de sectores estratégicos, pues había que priorizar la \"producción nacional\", el consumo interno y el \"crecimiento horizontal\" en todo el país. A los guiños tranquilizadores a empresarios e inversores el tabasqueño añadía la promesa de, llegada la hora de acabar con la corrupción y los privilegios de los ex presidentes, \"hacer justicia sin venganza ni odio\". \"No voy a meter a Peña Nieto en la cárcel\", aseguró también durante la campaña.\nOtras tomas de postura eran: el rechazo a un Gobierno de gran coalición, es decir, abierto a ministros del PRI o el PAN; la creación de los mecanismos legales de la revocación de los mandatos electos y el desafuero de aquellos cargos públicos procesados por corrupción; la provisión de Internet libre y gratuito en todo el territorio nacional; el cierre de las brechas de desigualdad, sobre todo en el ámbito laboral, entre hombres y mujeres; el programa de becas estudiantiles\nJóvenes Construyendo el Futuro\n; o la puesta en servicio de un Sistema Aeroportuario del Valle de México no basado en el proyecto del Nuevo Aeropuerto Internacional de México (NAIM), polémico por sus exorbitantes sobrecostes y su impacto medioambiental, sino en la habilitación del Aeropuerto Internacional de Santa Lucía (AISL) a partir de unas instalaciones militares ya existentes.\nEl 1 de abril de 2018 López Obrador, rezumando optimismo, abrió en Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, su tercera campaña presidencial en 12 años y el 27 de junio la cerró en un Estado Azteca, enorme cancha con capacidad para 87.000 espectadores de la Ciudad de México, lleno hasta la bandera y bañado en euforia. En las filas morenistas había ambiente de celebración por anticipado del triunfo electoral. Y no podía ser menos, a tenor de las encuestas, algunas de las cuales otorgaban a López Obrador más del 50% de los votos.\nTras cerrarse las urnas el domingo 1 de julio, el INE publicó el conteo rápido del PREP, que no dejaba dudas sobre la magnitud de la victoria, aplastante, de López Obrador. Al candidato opositor y virtual presidente electo le bastaron estos resultados preliminares para dirigir un primer mensaje desde el cuartel electoral de MORENA en el Hotel Hilton de la capital. Allí, bajo un gran rótulo que decía \"Gracias, México, no les voy a fallar\", López Obrador agradeció a sus oponentes el rápido reconocimiento de su triunfo en este \"día histórico\", llamó \"a todos los mexicanos a la reconciliación\", prometió \"erradicar\" la corrupción, \"que no es un fenómeno cultural, sino el resultado de un régimen en decadencia\", y tendió la mano a Trump, ofreciéndole \"una relación de amistad y cooperación para el desarrollo, siempre afincada en el respeto mutuo y en la defensa de nuestros paisanos que viven y trabajan honradamente en Estados Unidos\". Precisamente, Trump publicó en Twitter un cordial mensaje de felicitación y buena disposición para su flamante par mexicano.\n\nA continuación, López Obrador y su comitiva de colaboradores y familiares se trasladaron al Zócalo, donde les esperaban una muchedumbre enfervorizada, lista para escuchar el discurso de la victoria hasta bien entrada la madrugada del lunes 2 de julio. A sus seguidores,\nAMLO\nles garantizó la aplicación de \"los tres principios básicos: no mentir, no robar y no traicionar al pueblo\", anunció una \"transición con armonía\", desarrollada \"de manera ordenada, pacífica\", y prometió que los cambios iban a ser \"profundos, pero con apego al orden legal establecido\". \"Escucharemos a todos, atenderemos a todos, respetaremos a todos, pero daremos preferencia a los más humildes y olvidados; en especial, a los pueblos indígenas de México. Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres, dijo el orador, que recalcó también: \"Bajo ninguna circunstancia, el próximo presidente permitirá la corrupción ni la impunidad. Sobre aviso no hay engaño: sea quien sea, será castigado. Incluyo a compañeros de lucha, funcionarios, amigos y familiares\".\nEl 8 de julio, una vez completados los cómputos distritales, el INE publicó los resultados finales del escrutinio, que concedían la Presidencia a López Obrador con el 53,19% de los votos, habiendo alcanzado la participación el 64,4% del censo. Anaya había quedado segundo con el 22,27%, Meade tercero con el 16,40% y el independiente Jaime Rodríguez Calderón cuarto con el 5,23%. El morenista había sido el más votado en todos los estados salvo Guanajuato, decantado por Anaya. El 8 de agosto, por ultimo, el TEPJF dictaminó la validez de todo el proceso electoral y entregó la constancia de mayoría al ganador, haciéndose oficial su condición de presidente electo.\nLos resultados de las elecciones al Congreso de la Unión y de las celebradas en la mayoría de los estados terminaron de dibujar el alcance de la victoria de MORENA, comparable a un tsunami, y la derrota del PRI, calificable de colapso. El próximo Gobierno de López Obrador iba a gozar de mayoría absoluta en los dos hemiciclos federales: en la Cámara de Diputados, los tres partidos de Juntos Haremos Historia sumaban 308 escaños de 500 y en el Senado 69 escaños de 128. De las nueve gubernaturas sometidas a renovación el 1 de julio, MORENA se llevó las de la Ciudad de México (para Claudia Sheinbaum), Chiapas (Rutilio Escandón), Tabasco (Adán Augusto López) y Veracruz (Cuitláhuac García), mientras que su aliado el PES (Cuauhtémoc Blanco) se hizo con la de Morelos. El PAN, por su parte, retuvo los ejecutivos de Guanajuato y Puebla, y arrebató al PRI el de Yucatán, lo mismo que el Movimiento Ciudadano el de Jalisco. En los comicios a los congresos de 27 estados, MORENA fue la fuerza más votada 18, quedo segunda en siete, tercera en uno y cuarta en otro.\n(Cobertura informativa hasta 6/8/2018).\nMás información:\nWeb de Andrés Manuel López Obrador\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en X\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en Facebook\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en YouTube\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en Instagram\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en Telegram\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en TitTok\nAndrés Manuel López Obrador en Spotify\nPresidente de México\nPortal del Gobierno de México\nMovimiento Regeneración Nacional (MORENA)\nCIDOB es un centro de investigación en relaciones internacionales que, basándose en los criterios de excelencia y relevancia, tiene como objetivo el análisis de las cuestiones globales que afectan las dinámicas políticas, sociales y la gobernanza, desde lo internacional a lo local.\nPie de página\nSobre CIDOB\nInvestigación\nPublicaciones\nActualidad\nActividades", "excerpt_sha256": "b0c7140e54e6db453500fb7e557607b85700e19f671974c68a4ad7fc636abee5", "verification_status": "corrected", "verification_notes": ["The excerpt does not specify civilian command for the National Guard; result-oriented purposes in 2023, but 19% had none and 12% needed improvement. Half measured results adequately, while four needed indicator adjustments and four did not measure results. Logical linkage between components and purposes existed in six programs, needed strengthening in eight, and was absent in two. Universities for Wellbeing worsened from 'needs improvement' in 2021 to 'no results orientation' in 2023; Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro improved its component design, while Producción para el Bienestar worsened in logical linkage.", "question_ids": ["5B.7", "6B.5", "8B.1"], "polarity": "mixed", "period_fit": "Direct 2023 assessment with 2021-2023 comparisons.", "ruler_attribution": "The findings concern federal program purposes and indicators under the administration, not a demonstrated personal decision by López Obrador.", "limitations": ["The assessment evaluates program logic and indicators, not the full range of actual outcomes.", "Changes may reflect agency-level revisions, technical processes, or political direction; the source does not disaggregate causes."], "start_unit": 33, "end_unit": 39, "locator": "page 33 through page 39", "exact_excerpt": "Una vez que se presentó el panorama general de los programas prioritarios en 2023, es decir, cuáles\n     están vigentes en este año, a cuánto asciende su presupuesto asignado, cuál es su población objeti-\n     vo, qué temáticas de atención abordan y su cobertura, los siguientes capítulos de este informe repor-\n     tan los resultados de los análisis particulares de monitoreo que se llevaron a cabo para el seguimiento\n     de sus resultados, su presupuesto y su cumplimiento de metas. En este sentido, el objetivo del presente\n     capítulo es exponer la valoración del EdR13 de los 16 programas prioritarios.\n\n\n     El objetivo del EdR es evaluar si las MIR de los programas sociales identifican de forma clara y delimita-\n     da una población objetivo y el cambio sustancial que se espera en esta; si los indicadores del nivel de\n     Propósito miden dichos cambios y que los bienes y servicios (Componentes) son necesarios y suficien-\n     tes para el cumplimiento del objetivo central del programa. De esta forma, el análisis del EdR se realiza\n     a partir de tres categorías: a) Orientación a Resultados (OR) (valora la población objetivo y el cambio\n     en esta), b) Medición de Resultados (MR) (valora los indicadores de Propósito) y c) Asociación Lógica\n     (AL) (valora los Componentes de forma individual y en su conjunto).\n\n\n     Orientación a Resultados\n\n     La gráfica 7 muestra que la calificación para los 16 programas prioritarios es favorable, pues 69 % (11)\n     cuenta con OR en su objetivo de Propósito. Por su parte, 12 % (2) debe mejorar su OR, ya sea porque\n     aún no identifica adecuadamente su población objetivo o porque el cambio sustancial que espera\n     ver en esta no es claro. Por último, 19 % (3) de los programas prioritarios no cuentan con OR en sus\n     objetivos centrales. Aunque es una cifra baja, los programas prioritarios son la estrategia con la cual\n     la APF actual busca apoyar a los grupos más vulnerables de México. Su relevancia es tal, que es im-\n     prescindible continuar trabajando con estos programas hasta que logren identificar la población que\n     buscan atender y el cambio al que aspiran.\n\n\n     Gráfica 7. Objetivo central Orientado a Resultados de los programas prioritarios en 2023\n\n\n\n\n                                                   19 % (3)\n                                                                                                             El programa cuenta con OR\n\n\n                                                                                                             El programa debe mejorar su OR\n                                            12 % (2)\n                                                                            69 % (11)\n                                                                                                             El programa no cuenta con OR\n\n\n\n\n     Fuente: elaboración del CONEVAL.\n\n     13\n          El CONEVAL publica el Informe de Enfoque de Resultados en los años impares. Con base en esta valoración, se identifican áreas de mejora para que los programas y acciones\n          de desarrollo social se orienten correctamente al logro de resultados y cuenten con indicadores apropiados para medirlos.\n\n\n\n\n33    Informe de monitoreo de programas prioritarios 2023\n      Consejo Nacional de Evaluación de la Política de Desarrollo Social\n\nPor su parte, la gráfica 8 plasma la evolución en la OR de los programas prioritarios en el ciclo 2021-\n     2023. Como se evidencia, el número de programas que cuenta con OR se mantiene sin cambios. No\n     obstante, en el transcurso del ciclo de análisis, de los cinco programas prioritarios que deben mejorar\n     su OR o no cuentan con OR, solo se modificó el objetivo central de U083 “Universidades para el Bien-\n     estar Benito Juárez García” (SEP). En específico, este programa empeoró su dictamen al pasar de la\n     categoría que indica que debe mejorar su OR en 2021 a no contar con OR en 2023, pues con las\n     modificaciones a su objetivo central falló en la identificación adecuada de su población objetivo y el\n     cambio sustancial que esperaba lograr.\n\n\n     Gráfica 8. SUMMARY OF PROGRAM IMPLEMENTATION\nProgram and Portfolio Performance\n13. World Bank lending to Mexico has increased, driven by high growth in policy lending. IBRD lending\nhas increased by more than 25 percent in this CPF period relative to the previous one (FY14-19), propelled\nby an eightfold increase in DPF net commitments. At the end of FY23, total approved lending during the CPF\nperiod was US$4.3 billion (US$3.9 billion in DPF), versus US$3.4 billion during the previous CPF (US$0.5 billion\nin DPF). One additional DPF is planned for FY24. IFC’s commitments increased from US$1.62 billion in FY14-\n17 to US$1.75 billion in FY20-23. Annex 5 provides an overview of portfolio performance.\n14. Higher demand for policy lending and reduced appetite for investment lending can be traced to a\ncombination of global challenges and domestic policy shifts. Multiple global crises made fast-disbursing DPF\noperations the instrument of choice. Domestically, policy priorities were focused on a few large public\ninvestment projects, limiting space in the federal budget for other CPF focus areas. The government also\nwithdrew earlier requests for World Bank support in several areas, indicating shifting priorities or views of\nthe benefits of external project financing. Changing policy directions, institutional challenges, high turnover\nin key institutions, and security obstacles further affected policy continuity, implementation, and results.\nWith the 2024 electoral transition approaching, the window of opportunity for new policy reforms and the\npreparation of any further IPF pipeline is now limited.29\n15. The World Bank showed flexibility and pragmatism to deliver results through two main\nengagement strategies. First, IBRD responded to changing policy priorities by focusing on policy lending\nduring COVID-19 while continuing to invest in selected shared priorities: forestry preservation, financial\ninclusion, an improved business environment, and gender equality. IFC introduced upstream pre-investment\nprograms to support market creation and project structuring from an early stage, complemented by advisory\nprojects on climate, gender, and digitalization. Second, at client request, several investment operations were\nrestructured by the Bank, with cancellations of US$894 million out of US$1.28 billion in net commitments.\n16. The World Bank has maintained a strong analytical program to inform DPFs, to add value where\nmore intensive financial engagement was not possible, and to explore new entry-points. Demand-driven\nAdvisory Services and Analytics (ASA) informed key issues across the CPF objectives and maintained World\nBank engagement in many areas in the absence of lending (e.g., education, labor market policy, climate\nchange). The Reimbursable Advisory Services (RAS) instrument – a powerful instrument for middle-income\ncountries like Mexico – has been deployed in the transport sector, with a new agreement signed in July 2023.\n17. The CPF’s intended subnational focus on Mexico’s southern states was advanced through policy\nlending and advisory services. The CPF aimed for a greater impact on Mexico’s southern states, where a\nlarge share of the poorest population lives. This objective was affected by the reduced IPF program to\nchannel further resources to the poorest states in the south, as legal and institutional obstacles prevent direct\nlending to subnational government in Mexico. Still, IBRD supported federal policies (through policy-based\nlending) that generated benefits for the whole country, but had positive effects for lagging states (e.g., the\nUrban Upgrading Program supported under the Environmental Sustainability and Urban Resilience DPF\ntargeted marginalized urban areas with above-average deficits in access to public services and infrastructure\nin southern states). Analytical and advisory engagements have allowed demand-driven support to states, for\nexample through just-in-time support in several sectors (e.g., productivity, education, disaster risk\nmanagement), helping identify new partners and pave the way for potential future engagements (Annex 5).\n18. Fiduciary management has been satisfactory. Financial management and procurement\narrangements for IBRD projects are adequate. IBRD has strengthened client procurement capacity and\n29 The choice of lending instrument also relates to the characteristics of the investment project financing (IPF) instrument, particularly\nits disbursement profile, associated commitment fees and implementation modalities.\n4\n\nharmonized procurement documents are being updated.30 IBRD has also supported higher quality financial\nmanagement at national and project levels, in coordination with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)\nand the national organized accounting profession. Audits are generally on time and unqualified. More\ncustomized, agile approaches, including greater use of digital technologies, will be explored.\n19. The portfolio complied with safeguard policies and the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF).\nProject environmental and social risk ratings have ranged from moderate to low. Targeted supervision and\ncapacity-strengthening for all IPF projects have advanced ESF implementation, including in good practices\nsuch as the Dedicated Grant Mechanism for Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities Project.\n20. IFC’s committed portfolio in Mexico stands at US$2.4 billion, leveraging further private-sector\nfinance. As of December 31st, 2023, IFC portfolio included US$827 million of mobilized resources, the fourth\nlargest portfolio regionally and 13th globally. From FY20 to February 2024, IFC has committed US$2.3 billion\nof long-term financing (including US$900 million of mobilized resources) and US$706 million of short-term\nfinancing.\n21. MIGA’s guarantees in Mexico stand at US$2.3 billion, de-risking foreign investments and lending,\nwhich could lead the way to structure more operations with the financial sector. Mexico is MIGA’s largest\nexposure in the LAC region and globally. As of end-FY23, MIGA’s exposure in Mexico was in support of one\nproject in the energy sector. During the CPF, MIGA has provided guarantees to the Federal Electricity\nCommission to rehabilitate and modernize hydropower plants and to the export credit agency Bancomext to\nhelp exporting firms mitigate the impacts of the pandemic, the latter cancelled in April 2023. In October 2023,\nMIGA issued capital optimization guarantees of $1.9 billion to HSBC, covering the risk of expropriation of\nfunds for the mandatory reserves that HSBC Mexico holds at the central bank of Mexico.\nProgress Towards CPF Objectives\n22. Despite progress, many CPF targets are not on track. The global and domestic shifts described above\nhave both affected CPF implementation and results. Of 24 objective indicators, (i) eight have been achieved,\n(ii) one is partially achieved, (iii) five are on track but require adjustments to be achieved, and (iv) ten are off\ntrack, five of which are unlikely to be achieved as a result of cancellations or restructurings.31 In some areas,\nprogress has been made through other channels, e.g., DPF or ASA as opposed to IPF (see Annexes 3 and 5).\nFocus Area A: Supporting more rapid, more inclusive growth.\n23. In Focus Area A, of six indicators, one is achieved, one is partially achieved, one is on track, and\nthree are off track. Challenges are mainly due to cancellations and restructurings of operations, pandemic\nimpact, and monetary tightening to contain inflation.\n24. Financial intermediation and inclusion results are mixed. Progress on expanding access to credit for\nMSMEs was constrained by the pandemic, as well as liquidity and solvency issues faced by non-banking\nfinancial institutions (Indicator 1.2: MSMEs loans extended). Additional IBRD financing of the “Expanding\nRural Finance Project” was ruled out by debt ceilings during the pandemic and a shift in policy and lending\npriorities (Indicator 1.1: rural microenterprises and SMEs with access to credit). Financial inclusion has been\nexpanded through electronic payments via the new electronic payment platform (Indicator 1.3).\n25. IBRD has supported subnational competition regulation in the telecom, transport, and retail\nsectors. Forty-one subnational laws and regulations were changed to introduce a more competitive\nregulatory framework, achieving Indicator 2.1 (pro-competitive regulatory framework at the subnational\n30 Seven IPFs, including four trust funds are implementing the procurement regulations, taking into account the benefits of their\nflexibilities according to the context, risk, value, and complexity of each project, supported by its own project procurement strategy.\n31 Achieved: the targets were met on time or ahead of time; Partially achieved: half of the targets or less were met and the indicator\nis dropped in the PLR; On track: more than half of the targets have been met; Off track: half of the targets or less have been met.\n5\n\nlevel). IBRD also supported the conceptualization and design of the national digital platform aimed at\nenhancing business regulation across the regulatory governance cycle. IFC support to Altan Redes (the\ncompany responsible for the shared network) contributed to an increase in the population covered by\nwireless broadband to 70 percent as of January 2022 (Indicator 2.2). Limited progress was observed on\nagriculture storage infrastructure and market price information systems (Indicator 2.3), as a result of the\nJanuary 2020 cancellation of the “Grain Storage and Information for Agricultural Competitiveness Project” at\nclient request, reflecting changes in priorities. A strong ASA program on inclusive growth included the 2022\nProductivity Report and joint IBRD-IFC work on nearshoring, entrepreneurship, and eco-industrial parks.\nFocus Area B: Strengthening institutions for public finance, service delivery, and economic inclusion.\n26. In Focus Area B, of nine indicators, three have been achieved, one is on track, and five are off track.\nOn public service delivery, under Objective 3 (enhance the management of public resources), no progress\nwas made on Indicator 3.1 (population captured by the single identification system) due to the client decision\nto cancel the “National Digital Identity System Project” in 2022, reflecting priority changes. Support to public\nfinance through the “Modernization of Public Financial Management Systems in Mexico Project” was\nconstrained by the pandemic and implementation delays, which limited progress on Indicators 3.2 (budget\nexecuted through the Integrated Financial Management Information System) and 3.3 (time to produce\nconsolidated budget execution information). The project was restructured and is now in problem project\nstatus. IFC’s support to Public Private Partnership (PPP) transactions included two projects successfully\nawarded in May 2021 under the Los Cabos Water Advisory Project (Indicator 3.4: PPP transactions).\n27. Despite the impact of the pandemic, specific results indicators in education and social protection\nservice delivery are encouraging. Objective 4 (strengthen institutional capacity to deliver inclusive social\nservices) has been supported through the national early childhood development strategy (indicator 4.1\nadoption at the state level). Indicator 4.2 (pilots of the new integrated health networks at the state level) was\nnot achieved due to changes in government priorities. IBRD technical assistance was provided to the National\nInstitute of Public Health and the Secretariat of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP). Almost 52,000 additional\npatients were attended between 2018 and 2022 by IFC supported healthcare services, exceeding the targets\nfor Indicator 4.3 (patients benefiting from the healthcare services). Objective 5 (strengthen the capacity of\nthe social protection system for economic inclusion) was achieved through the “Social Protection System\nProject” and support to Mexico’s National Employment Service (SNE). Indicator 5.1 (Integrated Social\nProtection Centers established) was surpassed. Indicator 5.2 (implementation of modernized processes at\nSNE) has also been achieved through support to SNE, including the expansion of its office network.\nFocus Area C: Enabling sustainable infrastructure and climate action.\n28. In Focus Area C four of the nine objective indicators have been achieved; three are on track (after\nsome adjustments); and two are off track. Notable results have been achieved on housing and sustainable\nlandscape management, despite some implementation delays and restructuring.\n29. Progress has been lower than expected under Objective 6 on more inclusive and sustainable\ninfrastructure services. The “Water Security and Resilience of the Valley of Mexico Project” (PROSEGHIR),\napproved in February 2020, was delayed for over two years, slowing progress on Indicator 6.2 (people with\nimproved water supply reliability), but remains a priority in line with the Evolution Roadmap’s global\nchallenge on water security and access. A project to support Mexico’s National Infrastructure Fund\n(FONADIN) was dropped during preparation, affecting Indicator 6.1 (private capital mobilization for\ninfrastructure). Nevertheless, almost US$570 million have been mobilized by the issuance of sustainable\nbonds with a gender perspective by the infrastructure development bank, BANOBRAS. Despite US$800\nmillion of IFC additional private finance mobilization and own account investments in infrastructure, results\nare below expectations for indicator 6.1. MIGA’s guarantee played a catalytic role in the Tierra Mojada Power\nPlant project, which was cancelled in December 2020 owing to the successful refinancing of the project’s\n6\n\nbank debt with a bond, issued after the project had become operational. Although minimum power was\ndelivered during MIGA’s contract period, the project has generated 5,828 GWh of electricity above the target\nfor Indicator 6.4 (total power generated). In June 2023, MIGA also signed a guarantee supporting CFE for the\nrehabilitation and modernization of hydropower plants. The “Energy Efficiency in Public Facilities Project”\n(PRESEMEH) was scaled down to one third of the original US$150 million, reducing progress on Indicators 6.3\n(energy savings) and 7.1 (GHG emissions reduced). Indicator 6.5 (access to low-cost resilient housing) was\nreached through the “Improving Access to Affordable Housing Project” and IFC support to a housing provider.\n30. Progress on Objective 7 on climate change mitigation has been satisfactory. Sustainable landscape\nmanagement practices (Indicator 7.2) and the number of beneficiaries, particularly women and indigenous\npeoples, implementing sustainable management schemes (Indicator 7.3) have increased with satisfactory\nimplementation of the “Strengthening Entrepreneurship in Productive Forest Landscapes Project”\n(PROFOEM). Similarly, power generated from renewable energy sources supported by IFC has achieved its\ntarget (Indicator 7.4), with potential for further support. Indicators 7.1 (GHG emissions) and 7.3 (sustainable\nmanagement schemes in rural areas) were affected by restructurings of the forest, sustainable landscapes,\nand energy projects, but remain a priority to help tackle the global challenge of climate change.\nProgress Towards Corporate Commitments\n31. Corporate commitments have been mainstreamed across World Bank operations. The portfolio has\nexceeded corporate and regional targets since FY21 with 100 percent of IBRD projects gender-tagged and all\nactive projects complying with citizen engagement requirements. On climate, IBRD reached an average of\n41.3 percent of co-benefits in FY21-23, and IFC and MIGA had an average of 54.5 and 44.0 percent\nrespectively of new projects and guarantees tagged as climate-related since FY20 (Annex 6).\nPartnerships and Leveraging\n32. The World Bank has deepened coordination with other development partners. Under the\n“Environment Sustainability and Urban Resilience DPF” prior actions on climate, forests, and environmental\nmanagement were coordinated with partners (Annex 5). The Partnership for Market Implementation, a\nmulti-donor initiative led by the World Bank,32 has provided technical assistance on carbon pricing. The\nUnited Kingdom, the United States, and IBRD have joined forces to support Mexico’s forestry program\n(Objective 7). For the remainder of the CPF, closer collaboration within the WBG and with the IDB is expected,\nincluding on selected global challenges and private capital mobilization.\nIV. EMERGING LESSONS\n33. CPF design needs to adjust to the policy framework and operating environment, taking a\npragmatic, flexible, and creative approach to opportunities and risks. A realistic assessment of country\ncontext – policy priorities, financing constraints, political economy, and implementation capacity and\nlikelihood – is crucial. While the pandemic was impossible to predict, other governance, institutional, and\nsectoral risks could have been assessed more realistically and the program designed accordingly. The PLR\nbuilds on these lessons, with greater program selectivity and a more realistic risk assessment, seeking\nopportunities and balancing what is desirable with what is politically and technically possible at the federal,\nsubnational and sector levels. The Evolution Roadmap, with an enhanced value proposition for middle-\nincome countries, opens opportunities for a more integrated one World Bank Group approach at the project\nlevel and in joint knowledge engagements, such as on nearshoring, climate finance, financial inclusion, digital,\nenergy supply reliability and water. Global knowledge initiatives (e.g., the World Development Report on\nmigration) under the new Knowledge Compact may open doors to new forms of collaboration.\n34. Policy-lending can provide rapid support in response to crises, helping finance public expenditures\n32 Among them the European Commission, Germany, Spain, Sweden, Japan, United Kingdom, United States, and Australia.\n7\n\nand laying the foundations for a resilient recovery, while fostering innovations. In recent decades, Mexico\nhas followed a pattern of countercyclical lending, increasing exposure in downturns and crises (e.g., new\ncommitments of US$10.5 billion in FY08-10 and US$3.6 billion FY20-22). During COVID-19, three of four DPFs\napproved in FY20-22 directly supported pandemic crisis response and recovery, including the first “Build Back\nBetter” DPF. DPFs also supported innovative policy reforms (e.g., fintech, gender, and sustainable finance).\n35. IPF preparation can be challenging and fragile, yet investment lending operations have usually led\nto positive outcomes when implemented. Despite an investment pipeline reflecting the strength of the\ndialogue in many sectors, the government made a series of decisions not to proceed with many IPF\noperations. Complex project design, including inter- and intra-institutional coordination challenges,\nimplementation delays, partial cancellations, have jeopardized impact. Of the five IPF projects that closed in\nFY20-23, three were found satisfactory by the IEG (e.g., simple project design and client ownership\ncontributed to successful implementation). Four additional IPF projects are rated moderately satisfactory or\nbetter and are expected to achieve their objectives by closing in FY25. Reduced appetite for IPF and\nrestrictions on the use of this and other instruments (e.g., PforR) call for a close dialogue on design features,\nimplementation challenges, lessons learned to develop a new federal and potential also subnational pipeline.\n36. Analytical work has added technical value to policy making and served as a technical foundation\nfor policy lending. In the absence of new investment lending, the ASA program has positioned the World\nBank as a trusted adviser on evidence-based policy reforms, strengthening DPF design. Expansion of financial\naccess in Mexico was supported through the Financial Inclusion DPF, the COVID-19 Financial Access DPF, and\nthe Promoting Women’s Economic Opportunities and Sustainable Productivity Growth DPF. These operations\nbuilt on the 2016 and 2022 Financial Sector Assessment Programs, the Financial Inclusion Global Initiative,\nthe Gender Report, and IFC support on business regulations and SME access to credit.\n37. For IFC, deepening the relationship with the Ministry of Finance, diversifying business\ndevelopment efforts across industries and client types, while also emphasizing non-financial benefits, is\nexpected to both mitigate sector concentration risk and strengthen IFC’s value proposition. IFC investments\nin renewable energy in Mexico have grown substantially, representing almost 100 percent of new IFC\ninfrastructure investments from FY18 to FY20. Subsequent difficulties in the sector created a shock to IFC’s\ninfrastructure target, which was only partially mitigated by increased support for digital infrastructure. IFC’s\ndiversification to new players within the financial system and its use of the highest environmental, social, and\ngovernance standards have enhanced IFC’s contribution to the financial inclusion and climate agenda,\nincluded under CPF focus areas A and C. The latter can be illustrated by IFC investments in the Sustainable\nBond issued by GF Mega, structured under a sustainability framework to promote financial inclusion,\nwomen’s empowerment, and climate-friendly practices; and the Partial Credit Guarantee to IDEI Green Bond\nIssuance, to finance Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies (EDGE)-certified green residential projects.\nSynergies and complementarities among IFC, IBRD, and MIGA can also strengthen product and market\ndiversification.\nV. ADJUSTMENTS TO COUNTRY PARTNERSHIP FRAMEWORK\n38. This PLR confirms the strategic direction and the duration of the CPF but proposes adjustments to\nthe results framework. The PLR confirms that the three CPF Focus Areas remain appropriate to address\nMexico’s structural growth, inclusion, and sustainability challenges identified in the Systematic Country\nDiagnostic.33 The PLR adjusts Objective 2 to reflect new engagements with the private sector and drops\nObjective 3 to reflect implementation delays and cancellations. Objective 2 includes new indicators on the\nadoption of a framework to certify industrial parks. Focus Area 3 will continue supporting Mexico in some of\nthe most pressing global challenges, e.g., Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation; Energy Access; and\nWater Security and Access. The results matrix has been streamlined to reflect reform space, client demand,\n33 World Bank, “Mexico Systematic Country Diagnostic,” August 2019.\n8\n\nand implementation capacity by sector34 (Annex 2).\nFocus Area A: Supporting more rapid, more inclusive growth.\n39. The PLR maintains Objective 1 to “foster financial intermediation and inclusion” and continues\nsupporting sustainable finance. With limited space for new lending, the PLR proposes to support Mexico’s\nsustainable finance agenda through analytical support, including the development of a biodiversity taxonomy\nand associated regulations, building on the joint IFC-IBRD 30x30 Zero advisory services, which also aims to\nraise the share of green assets in bank portfolios. On financial intermediation, new objectives have been\nadded on increasing account ownership and reducing the gender gap in digital payments. Indicators on users\nand payments through the digital payments’ platform and MSME loans have been revised to reflect progress.\n40. Objective 2 is adjusted from aiming to “reduce regulatory and competition barriers to economic\ngrowth” to “support private sector investment.” IBRD will support ASA on the subnational implementation\nof a national digital platform to improve business regulation. Based on analytical work on productivity,\nentrepreneurship, and eco-industrial parks, IBRD and IFC will support FDI attraction for the piloting of eco-\nindustrial parks. The PLR includes two new indicators on a framework to certify industrial parks including\nenvironmental sustainability and the number of IFC transactions tagged as “nearshoring.”\nFocus Area B: Strengthening institutions for service delivery and inclusion.\n41. Focus Area B is adjusted from “Strengthening institutions for public finance, service delivery, and\neconomic inclusion” to “Strengthening institutions for service delivery and inclusion.” The PLR drops\nObjective 3 to “enhance the management of public resources” due to project implementation delays and\ncancellations. IBRD will continue supporting SHCP plans to strengthen human resource and public investment\nmanagement and its integration with the budget system as well as the implementation of Mexico’s\nsustainable finance strategy. IFC will continue structuring and financing PPP projects in key sectors, yet with\nmore limited scope, given reduced federal funding to structure projects and uneven subnational capacities.\n42. Objective 4 (new Objective 3) is revised to “strengthen the capacity to deliver inclusive education\nand health services.” IBRD will remain engaged in early childhood education and support the recovery of\nlearning losses by (i) improving teaching practices; (ii) developing early warning systems to identify students\nat risk of dropping out and targeted efforts to lower this risk; and (iii) catalyzing human capital formation by\nexpanding early childhood care and education services. IFC will continue to support innovative, scalable\nmodels for high-quality, affordable private health-care services. In line with the pandemic prevention and\npreparedness global challenge, IBRD has shifted its engagement to formulating proposals to enhance\nreadiness and responses for health crises and the resilience of health financing to population ageing.\n43. Objective 5 (new Objective 4) is adjusted to “strengthen the capacity to deliver inclusive social\nservices.” IBRD work with SNE to use good practices and digital tools to support social protection and\nimprove the integration of vulnerable members of the labor force (e.g., women, youth, and migrants).\nFocus Area C: Enabling sustainable infrastructure and climate action.\n44. Objective 6 (new Objective 5) on more inclusive and sustainable infrastructure services remains a\npriority, despite challenges in infrastructure sectors. In the water sector, IBRD will continue to support water\nsupply and sanitation activities through its operation in the Valley of Mexico and potential investments and\nadvisory work in the northern part of the country (e.g., wastewater treatment and reuse, groundwater\nmonitoring and management, and irrigation modernization) in line with the water security and access global\nchallenge. The energy efficiency project (PRESEMEH) will be closed. MIGA will expand its presence through\nits guarantee to CFE supporting efforts towards tackling the global challenge on energy efficiency and access.\nIBRD will support Mexico’s development banks on private sector capital mobilization, especially for\n34 The PLR drops nine, adjusts thirteen, and reconfirms two out of 24 objective indicators, and adds five new indicators.\n9\n\ninfrastructure and energy. IFC will support competitive private energy markets and digital infrastructure,\nfocusing on renewables and telecom, in addition to other areas where private investment can help meeting\nthe growing needs from nearshoring. WBG collaboration with financial entities and funds will be\nstrengthened to promote private capital mobilization to address infrastructure needs in key sectors such as\ntransport, energy, water, and real estate. Indicators have been adjusted to reflect progress and challenges.\n45. The World Bank will intensify efforts to support Mexico’s climate change goals under Objective 7\n(new Objective 6). Cross-sectoral climate change mitigation and adaptation, one of the key global challenges\noutlined in the Evolution Roadmap, will be supported through ASA. IFC will mobilize knowledge and\ninvestments targeted at financial institutions, fintech, and funds to develop sound climate portfolios. MIGA\nwill seek opportunities to support renewable energy projects. MIGA has also issued new capital optimization\nguarantees to HSBC covering the risk of expropriation of funds for the mandatory reserves that HSBC Mexico\nholds at the central bank of Mexico. The benefits of the MIGA-enabled capital relief will provide financing of\nUS$1.5 billion to climate finance sub-projects over 2023-2026. IBRD operations on forestry and agriculture\nwill continue with a focus on forest-dependent communities and on strengthening community and producer\norganizations in the management and entrepreneurship of productive landscapes, protecting biodiversity\nand nature as a key global challenge. The World Bank will seek innovation in financial solutions for disaster\nmanagement and climate resilience and support the sustainable taxonomy. Objectives have been adjusted.\nVI. RISKS TO THE CPF PROGRAM\n46. The overall risk for this CPF has increased from Moderate to Substantial. Table shows the risk\nassessment, using the Systematic Operations Risk-rating Tool (SORT). The World Bank will carefully assess\nand mitigate risks through the electoral transition to build a close engagement with the new administration.\nTable 1. SORT: Risks to the CPF program\nRisk categories CPF Rating PLR Rating\n47. Political and Governance Risk is\nPolitical and governance M S\nincreased from moderate to substantial.\nMacroeconomic M M\nSectoral strategies and policies S S Program implementation could be delayed\nTechnical design of projects or programs M M ahead of the presidential election in June\nInstitutional capacity for implementation 2024 and the following transition period,\nM S\nand sustainability\nincluding restrictions on new reforms. To\nFiduciary M M\nmitigate this risk, IBRD will focus on: (i)\nEnvironment and social M M\naccelerating portfolio implementation and\nStakeholders M M\nOther (crime and violence) S S addressing project risks; (ii) preparing a\nOverall M S transition engagement strategy (including\nNote: Summary risks: H = high; S = substantial; M = moderate; L = low transition notes) and rapidly engaging with\nthe new administration; and (iii) seeking opportunities for subnational dialogue.\n48. Institutional Capacity for Implementation and Sustainability risk has risen to substantial.\nImplementation challenges have increased, affecting planning, management, budgeting, and monitoring and\nevaluation. Turnover of government staff, limited experience with international financial institutions,\nprocess-intensive implementation, regulatory and bureaucratic hurdles, and procurement delays have\nincreased transaction times, requiring the restructuring of implementation arrangements in several projects.\nTo mitigate these risks, IBRD has strengthened the coordination with government, created early warning\nmechanisms across the portfolio, and enhanced implementation readiness on new investment projects.\n49. Insecurity, crime, and violence continue to pose substantial risks to CPF implementation. Security\nchallenges affect beneficiaries and staff, impede mission travel and delay operations. To mitigate the risks,\nengagements in high-risk areas are limited, remote monitoring is used, security is closely monitored, and\nsecurity training and support is provided in line with the Mexico Office Security Strategy.\n10", "excerpt_sha256": "b763926bac1a6c5b30325aa396d5673b862ca81e59b2591b1cc7ac00c8b67616", "verification_status": "accepted", "verification_notes": ["The excerpt directly supports the indicator counts, pandemic and institutional factors, client-requested restructurings/cancellations, and continued policy lending and analytical support."]}, {"evidence_id": "BATCH-0052-E020", "source_id": "SRC-240044c0f4fd6c00", "url": "https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099032124080524844/pdf/BOSIB15b3ebe810f518e201c5cfce8f25cd.pdf", "title": "Mexico Social Protection Public Expenditure and Institutional Review", "publisher": "World Bank", "raw_sha256": "5af01216a7eaa150c1c22653f14028213e569bb7de3bea266525c487ae7bc343", "fact_summary": "During FY2020-2023, the World Bank recorded a sharp shift toward policy lending, ten project closures, four partial cancellations, four projects dropped during preparation, and two unsigned loan offers. Program Implementation\nProgram and Portfolio Performance\n1. World Bank lending to Mexico has increased. As of December 2023, the World Bank active\nportfolio includes US$1.68 billion from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development\n(IBRD), US$2.4 billion committed portfolio from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and US$536\nmillion from the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA). Under the current CPF, the total\nIBRD lending approved sums up to US$4.3 billion (US$1.1 billion average per year) relative to US$560.0\nmillion in the previous CPF. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) also committed investments\nincreased in the first four years relative to the same period of the previous CPF, from US$1.62 billion\nduring FY14-17 to US$1.75 billion during FY20-23. Responding to global context and increased client\nappetite for countercyclical financing sources, DPF increased to US$3.9 billion compared to US$0.5 billion\nunder the previous CPF.228 Over FY20-FY23, four Development Policy Financing (DPF) operations were\nextended to the Mexican authorities, three directly supporting the COVID-19 crisis response and\nrecovery, including IBRD’s first Build Back Better DPF. For FY24, the pipeline for the remaining CPF\nconsists of only one DPF project. In addition, IBRD has an active Bank-executed trust fund portfolio\nbenefiting the country which comprises 34 trust funds for a total net commitment of US$71.1 million.\n2. IBRD portfolio has moved from an average of sixteen projects during the previous CPF to ten\nprojects during the current CPF, with a gradual reduction of investment project financing (IPF). IPF was\nreduced from 11 projects in 2020 to 7 in 2023. The active IBRD portfolio as of December 2023, comprises\nfive IBRD loans (US$1.6 billion), complemented by two Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects, and\none recipient executed trust-funded project. Since the CPF was discussed by the Board, seven IBRD\nprojects and one GEF stand-alone project have been approved. During this same period, ten projects\nclosed, four operations were partially cancelled, four were prepared but dropped at later stages of\npreparation, and two were not signed resulting in withdrawn loan offers (Table 5.2).\nTable 5.1. World Bank Business Intelligence Reporting, Standard Reports, and Analysis for Office.\n4. A strong analytical program helped maintain the dialogue and explore entry-points for further\ncollaboration with the current and the next administration. Formal Advisory Services and Analytics (ASA),\nsuch as the Female Labor Force Participation Report,229 the Pensions Policy Support Program, and the\nProductivity Report,230 helped to set up the agenda, informing reform options and lending, such as in the\n“Promoting Women Economic Opportunities and Sustainable Productivity Growth DPF” operation. Just-\nin-time support, such as for the education, health, social protection and labor sectors, helped maintain\nthe dialogue and pave the ground for future engagements (e.g., an assessment of learning lost during\nschool closures). IBRD has become a key partner in assisting the authorities implement a comprehensive\nearly childhood education and development strategy; IBRD’s analytical support has been welcomed by\nthe Secretariat of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP) and health sector agencies to assess the sustainability\nand resilience of health financing in the face of shocks and population ageing; while Mexico has turned\nrepeatedly to IBRD’s Social Protection and Jobs practice for support on pension reform, modernizing its\nlabor market intermediation services and for support in integrating migrants into the economy. In\naddition, IBRD’s engagement focused strongly on helping the government advance the climate resilience,\nforestry, and land use agendas. As a result, in 2020 an innovative “Environmental Sustainability and Urban\nResilience DPF” was approved, which addressed development challenges around the increase of the\nresilience of the most vulnerable municipalities, the gradual reform towards non-deforestation criteria in\nagriculture support programs, and local air quality provisions to mitigate black carbon. Likewise, this DPF\nalso strongly featured IBRD’s urban engagement. Strong operational engagement in the water sector has\nbeen further supported by analytical work laying the foundation for strengthening IBRD’s engagement in\nthe sector at national and subnational levels. Engagements with the SHCP on disaster risk management,\ne.g., technical assistance to strengthen the risk management strategy related to natural hazard risk at the\nfederal and subnational levels, helped respond to core client demands and laid the foundation for longer-\nterm reforms on the Evolution Roadmap global challenges’ agenda. ASAs also led to demand in trust-funds\nand other concessional funding.\n5. Reimbursable Advisory Services are a powerful engagement instrument for middle-income\ncountries. A Reimbursable Advisory Services (RAS) agreement was signed in transport in June 2023 and\n229 World Bank, “Female Labor Force Participation in Mexico,” March 2021.\n230 World Bank, “Productivity Growth in Mexico: Understanding Main Dynamics and Key Drivers,” January 2022.\n67\n\nother RAS engagements were explored in line with sector demand in the education and health sectors but\ndid not materialize.\n6. Given legal challenges for direct lending to the sub-national level and security risks, IBRD relied\non ASA to support subnational. For example, IBRD has supported the municipalities of Tulum and San\nCristobal de las Casas in developing their Municipal Climate Action Plans, and in March 2023, launched a\ntechnical assistance program (financed by the Climate Investment Facility) to develop a city climate action\nplan for the metropolitan area of Oaxaca, including all the 25 municipalities, located in one of the\ncountry’s poorest states in the south.\n7. Similarly, advisory programs helped to keep a strong involvement from public and private\ninstitutions in priority areas such as climate. Under the 30x30 Zero project in Mexico, for instance,\nIFC/IBRD collaborated with Mexico’s Central Bank (Banxico), originally through the Sustainable Finance\nCommittee, part of the Financial Stability Board, to examine the different aspects of “greening the\nfinancial sector”: (i) Green Taxonomy, (ii) reporting and disclosure, (iii) social and climate risk analysis, and\n(iv) ecoefficiency and decarbonization. A gender agenda with financial institutions and regulators is being\ncarried out jointly by IFC and IBRD to address policy and market challenges to untap and scale new\nopportunities. IFC participated in the four working groups and supported the green Taxonomy, which\nbecame the Sustainable Taxonomy. Also, through the Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) Green\nBuildings program, IFC has supported the public and private sectors’ green agenda, reaching 4.9 million\nsquare meters certified with the Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies (EDGE) certificate, and\nthrough the TechEmerge Sustainable Cooling Cities program, the successful closure of 11 pilots by FY23\nwhere participants were able to decide on potential scale-up of innovate cooling solutions either at\nadopter or at broader market. This EDGE achievement positions Mexico as the third country globally with\nthe largest certified floor space. IBRD and IFC are also working together on how to harness nearshoring\ninvestments in Mexico for which a close coordination with the government would be key. Teams are\nworking on a strategy to leverage this opportunity to address development gaps (notably declining\nproductivity, high informality, asymmetric integration into global value chains, and low technological\nupgrade by local firms), while promoting a sustainable and inclusive approach of these investments and\npublic-private coordination to provide the enabling factors. MIGA is also planning to join those strategic\nconversation as one World Bank to explore opportunities to deploy MIGA de-risking solutions to enhance\nbankability of projects, facilitate public-private investments, and the mobilization of foreign capital in\nMexico. More specifically, the close collaboration with IBRD and IFC proved crucial in the development of\nthe Federal Commission Electricity (CFE) project, where MIGA provided non-honoring guarantees to a\nstate-owned utility, given rapidly evolving conditions in the energy sector.\"\n8. Portfolio management has incorporated fiduciary considerations. On procurement, tailored\nproject procurement strategies have been designed in line with each project’s context, risks, regulations,\nand complexities, allowing for flexibility and better execution of Procurement Plans, but also to overcome\nchallenges. These include misalignment of the procurement processes to optimize the use of resources in\ncontracts, and lack of government staff with experience conducting procurement processes financed with\nIBRD resources. Mitigation measures have included additional support to implementing entities, including\nin the use of innovative methods such as the use of rated criteria, and harmonization of procurement\ndocuments with the most recent country’s regulations and policies. Performance on financial\nmanagement continues to be generally satisfactory. Challenges related to budgeting and limited fiscal\nspace for investment operations, including trust funds, remain. IBRD loan proceeds are budgeted only on\nan annual basis, and grant funds cannot be received directly by federal entities, affecting planning and\ncausing implementation delays. Limited federal budgetary resources have also led to a reduction in the\nscope of some investment projects. To tackle these challenges, IBRD has continued to promote fiduciary\n68\n\ncapacity development for project-implementing entities through the provision of regular training (i.e., on\nIBRD’s systematic tracking of exchanges in procurement, STEP) and workshops (i.e., a fiduciary workshop\nheld in June 2023), and through actively engaging with the organized accounting profession in Mexico in\ncoordination with the Inter-American Development Bank.\n9. Safeguards ratings and environment and social (E&S) standards performance ranged between\nmoderately satisfactory and satisfactory, with no projects closed with pending E&S measures. IBRD has\nprovided oversight, supervision, follow-up, and capacity-building support, for all IPF projects. One of the\ninnovations of the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) is the recognition that climate change is\naffecting the nature and location of IBRD-financed projects. It sets out a vision to support client countries\nto decarbonize and invest in resilience to help overcome climate change as a fundamental threat to\ndevelopment in our lifetime. Although the requirement for new operations, the Paris Alignment\nassessment, is distinct from the E&S assessment set out in the ESF, the ESF’s standards reinforce the World\nBank’s ability to ensure financing aligns with the goals of the Paris Agreement.\n10. Complementing IBRD’s lending, IFC’s committed portfolio in Mexico stands at US$2.4 billion as\nof December 2023, helping leverage private sector financing. As of December 31st, 2023, IFC portfolio\nincluded US$827 million of mobilized resources, making this the fourth largest portfolio regionally and the\n13th globally. From FY20 to February 2024, IFC has committed US$2.3 billion of long-term financing\n(including US$900 million of mobilized resources) and US$706 million of short-term financing in Mexico.\nThe main transactions focused on expanding access to health through low-cost generic medicine,\nincreasing financial inclusion by supporting FinTech, insurance, and non-banking financial institutions,\nhelping job recovery in the tourism sector, promoting digital infrastructure by investing in data centers,\nand supporting renewable energy and green buildings.\nTable 5.5.
